slice: exploring: a retrovirus in a genome as a ghost

items.text: A retrovirus in a genome is a ghost: a field observes sequences in a genome now, reads them as an ancient infection's leaving, and installs one momentary's form, a virus particle entering a germ cell long ago, as an existing thing and an actor; that entering is a field's inference from comparing sequences, with no observing of it, and one part rides the genome's going on, which a still installing cannot contain: an early embryo's own cells transcribing these sequences, and placental cells fusing by syncytin genes.

items.section: 1.3 Every self is a same-existing-society of selves
items.text: About 8 percent of the human genome is sequence a field names endogenous retroviruses, most of it defective and only a few able to form virus particles; in human embryos three to four days old some HERV-K sequences are transcribing, and in blastocysts of five to six days electron microscopy shows what appear to be intact viral particles; HERV-K's Rec protein binds viral RNAs and also RNAs of human genes, and raises IFITM1, a protein that blocks viral infection; a HERV-H RNA binds proteins needed for embryonic stem cells to keep their stem-cell identity, and removing it loses stem properties.

items.section: 1.3 Every self is a same-existing-society of selves
items.text: Phylogenetic evidence suggests vertebrate retroviruses arise from genome elements, LTR retrotransposons, that move within a genome, the element first; a retrovirus has an extra envelope gene that mediates infection, and in three cases an envelope-like gene is from a virus: insect errantiviruses from baculoviruses, nematode Cer from phleboviruses, and Tas from herpesviruses, a weak case; a field infers this from comparing sequences and does not observe it.

items.section: 1.3 Every self is a same-existing-society of selves
items.text: Koala retrovirus is in each Queensland koala a test reaches, in some southern populations and in none on Kangaroo Island, its insertions varying in number and pattern between koalas; it has a full-length genome able to replicate and form particles and is a close relative of gibbon ape leukemia virus; a field reads it as entering koala genomes within the last 100 years, a reading from the koalas' population history and not from dating the entering.
